\begin{abstract}
Compound sparsity---simultaneously pruning attention heads and evicting KV cache entries---is essential for efficient LLM inference but produces super-additive quality degradation whose structure is poorly understood.
Prior work treats compound interaction magnitude as approximately constant across the generation process.
We show that this assumption is wrong: compound sparsity severity is an emergent phase-strategy interaction that varies by over an order of magnitude across reasoning phases.

We evaluate compound sparsity on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (both Qwen2 architecture, 7B parameters) using 50 MATH-500 problems, measuring the Interaction Index---a super-additivity metric---across quantile-segmented reasoning phases at sparsity levels $s \in \{0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30\}$.
Under importance-based KV cache eviction, the median Interaction Index difference between low-sparsity and high-sparsity reasoning phases increases monotonically from $0.39$ at $s{=}0.15$ to $14.59$ at $s{=}0.30$, with paired Cohen's $d_z$ growing from $0.44$ (small) to $0.80$ (large); Bonferroni-corrected permutation tests yield $p < 0.005$ at all four sparsity levels.
Random eviction produces no significant phase modulation in 7/8 conditions; the single exception (Qwen $s{=}0.30$, $p{=}0.012$) shows negligible effect size ($d_z{=}{-}0.04$), confirming that the severity gradient is strategy-specific, not an inherent property of compound sparsity.
At $s{=}0.25$, a crossover emerges: importance-based eviction outperforms random in high-sparsity phases ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}} = 0.032$ vs.\ $0.818$) yet underperforms in low-sparsity phases ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}} = 7.196$ vs.\ $1.363$)---a qualitative reversal in strategy ranking.
The pattern replicates on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct at $s \geq 0.20$ ($d_z \geq 0.55$; Spearman $\rho = 1.0$ across sparsity levels; gradient permutation $p = 0.043$).

We propose entropy-discrimination collapse as an explanatory mechanism: head pruning flattens cumulative importance scores in phases where attention is already broadly distributed, degrading the discriminative power of importance-based eviction in a phase-dependent manner.
These findings challenge the phase-invariance assumption in compound sparsity deployment and motivate phase-aware compression budgets for reasoning models.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Long-context language models place acute pressure on the key--value (KV) cache, which grows linearly with sequence length and dominates inference memory at scale \cite{kwon2023vllm, pope2023efficiently}.
Two complementary responses have emerged: \emph{attention head pruning}, which removes structurally redundant heads \cite{voita2019heads, michel2019sixteen}, and \emph{KV cache eviction}, which discards low-importance token positions from the cache \cite{snapkv-neurips2024, adakv-neurips2025}.
Deploying both simultaneously---\emph{compound sparsity}---is attractive because the compression gains multiply, but the resulting quality degradation can be super-additive: the joint loss exceeds the sum of individual losses \cite{spark-aaai2026, slim-icml2025}.

Prior work has characterized compound interaction as a property of the sparsity level---higher sparsity yields more interaction---but treats the interaction magnitude as roughly constant across the generation process \cite{spark-aaai2026, unicomp-2026}.
This assumption is problematic for reasoning-capable models, whose generations are structurally heterogeneous: a single chain-of-thought trace alternates between phases of broadly distributed attention (exploratory reasoning) and phases of sharply concentrated attention (structured computation) \cite{thinkv-iclr2026, decision-repr-transition-2026}.
If compound interaction severity varies across these phases, then a uniform sparsity budget---the standard deployment practice---may be safe in one phase yet destructive in another.

We investigate whether compound sparsity severity is modulated by reasoning phase and eviction strategy.
Our central finding is that it is, and strongly so: under importance-based KV cache eviction, the Interaction Index---a measure of super-additive compound degradation---is concentrated in the low-sparsity phase (where attention distributes broadly) and largely absent in the high-sparsity phase (where attention is focused).
This \emph{severity gradient} grows monotonically with the sparsity budget: on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, the median phase difference in Interaction Index rises from $0.39$ at $s{=}0.15$ to $14.59$ at $s{=}0.30$, with paired effect sizes increasing from $d_z{=}0.44$ (small) to $d_z{=}0.80$ (large); Bonferroni-corrected permutation tests confirm significance at all four sparsity levels on this model ($p < 0.005$).
The pattern replicates at $s \geq 0.20$ on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ($d_z \geq 0.55$) with attenuated absolute magnitude, though the effect at $s{=}0.15$ is marginal ($d_z{=}0.28$, bootstrap CI includes zero).
Critically, random eviction produces no such gradient: 7/8 conditions across both models fail to exhibit a significant phase difference (the single exception---Qwen $s{=}0.30$---has negligible effect size, $d_z{=}{-}0.04$), confirming that the severity gradient is an emergent property of the interaction between importance scoring and phase-dependent attention structure, not an artifact of compound sparsity per se.

We propose \emph{entropy-discrimination collapse} as an explanatory mechanism.
Head pruning forces surviving heads to redistribute attention mass, increasing attention entropy.
In low-sparsity phases, where attention is already broadly distributed, this redistribution flattens the cumulative importance scores used for KV eviction, degrading their discriminative power.
Importance-based eviction then degenerates into a biased pseudo-random process that can inadvertently remove critical positions---amplifying compound severity.
In high-sparsity phases, attention concentration is preserved after pruning, importance scores remain discriminative, and eviction remains well-targeted.
Random eviction is immune to this mechanism because its decisions are independent of attention patterns.

Our contributions are as follows:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item We identify a \textbf{phase--strategy interaction} in compound sparsity: importance-based eviction exhibits a severity gradient across reasoning phases that is absent under random eviction (\S\ref{sec:results}).
    \item We show that this severity gradient \textbf{increases monotonically with sparsity} and replicate the finding at moderate-to-high sparsity ($s \geq 0.20$) across two models with different training regimes (distillation vs.\ instruction tuning), establishing robustness within the Qwen2 architecture family (\S\ref{sec:results}).
    \item We propose \textbf{entropy-discrimination collapse} as a mechanistic explanation, linking head pruning to the degradation of importance-score discriminability in a phase-dependent manner (\S\ref{sec:analysis}).
\end{enumerate}

These findings challenge the implicit assumption that compound interaction magnitude is phase-invariant, and suggest that sparsity budgets should be allocated in a phase-aware manner---tightening compression during low-sparsity reasoning phases where compound interaction is most severe.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: \S\ref{sec:related} surveys related work on compound compression, KV cache eviction, and phase-aware inference; \S\ref{sec:background} formalizes compound sparsity and introduces the Interaction Index; \S\ref{sec:experimental-setup} describes our experimental setup; \S\ref{sec:results} presents the main results; \S\ref{sec:analysis} analyzes the entropy-discrimination collapse mechanism; and \S\ref{sec:discussion} discusses implications and limitations.

3	\label{sec:results}
4	
5	We present our empirical findings in five parts: strategy-dependent compound severity (\S\ref{sec:strategy-severity}), phase-modulated amplification (\S\ref{sec:phase-amplification}), the phase-strategy crossover (\S\ref{sec:crossover}), cross-model replication (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}), and statistical validation (\S\ref{sec:stat-validation}).

8	\subsection{Experimental Overview}
9	\label{sec:exp-overview}
10	
11	We evaluate compound sparsity on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B using a 50-problem stratified subset of MATH-500 under four conditions---dense, attention-only pruning, KV-only eviction, and compound---at sparsity levels $s \in \{0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30\}$, comparing importance-based and random eviction. The interaction index (II, Eq.~\ref{eq:ii}) quantifies compound super-additivity; the severity gradient ($G$, Eq.~\ref{eq:gradient}) captures phase-dependent amplification. Full setup in \S\ref{sec:experimental-setup}.

14	\subsection{Strategy-Dependent Severity (C1)}
15	\label{sec:strategy-severity}
16	
17	The compound severity difference reveals a stark dependence on eviction strategy. Table~\ref{tab:aggregate-ii} reports the median compound severity difference $\Delta = \widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\textit{low}} - \widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\textit{high}}$ across 50 problems for each strategy and sparsity level. Under importance-based eviction, compound sparsity produces substantial super-additive degradation that grows with sparsity: $\Delta$ increases from $0.39$ at $s{=}0.15$ to $14.59$ at $s{=}0.30$, a $37{\times}$ amplification. Under random eviction, the severity difference shows no systematic growth, remaining near zero ($-0.02$ to $1.54$). % exp_id: bf16_importance_s015..s030, bf16_ds_rand_s015..s030; source: experiment_summary_table.json

2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	\paragraph{On the predictability of phase-modulated severity.}
5	One might argue that the qualitative direction of our findings is intuitive: in low-sparsity phases, attention distributes broadly across many tokens, so importance scores carry less discriminative signal, and importance-based eviction should degrade.
6	We do not dispute this intuition.
7	The surprise lies in the quantitative structure of the interaction, which is not predictable from first principles alone.
8	
9	First, the \emph{magnitude} of the severity gradient---$69$--$274{\times}$ amplification across sparsity levels (Table~\ref{tab:main-results})---far exceeds what a naive ``less discriminative $\Rightarrow$ somewhat worse'' argument would predict. % exp_id: bf16_importance_s015..s030; source: experiment_summary_table.json; G=low/high=69,103,222,274.

34	The entropy-discrimination collapse hypothesis (\S\ref{sec:analysis}) receives partial cross-model support.

38	We therefore characterize the mechanistic evidence as \emph{preliminary}: the discrimination pathway is robust across models, but the complete entropy-discrimination collapse narrative requires the qualification that its entropy component does not generalize.
39	
40	\paragraph{Implications for compound sparsity deployment.}
41	Our findings suggest that the standard practice of applying a uniform compression budget across all inference steps is suboptimal for reasoning models.
42	Compound severity is not distributed evenly: it concentrates in low-sparsity phases, where the entropy-discrimination collapse mechanism (\S\ref{sec:analysis}) renders importance-based eviction unreliable.
43	A deployment pipeline that allocates the same sparsity level $s$ to every token position implicitly accepts order-of-magnitude severity penalties during the exploratory reasoning stages that happen to fall in the low-sparsity regime.
44	
45	This observation motivates \emph{phase-aware compression budgets}: rather than a single global sparsity target, the system would allocate higher capacity (lower sparsity) to low-sparsity phases---where compound interaction is most severe---and reclaim that budget in high-sparsity phases, where compound behavior is near-additive and importance-based eviction remains effective.
46	The severity gradient $G$ reported in \S\ref{sec:phase-amplification} provides a natural signal for such allocation: phases with $G \gg 1$ receive a reduced sparsity budget, while phases with $G \leq 1$ tolerate aggressive compression with minimal quality loss.
47	
48	\paragraph{Future directions.}
49	The phase-aware allocation principle above points toward a concrete system design: a \emph{phase-gated controller} that monitors attention sparsity statistics in real time and dynamically adjusts the compound sparsity budget per reasoning phase.
50	The controller would route each generation step through a low-overhead phase classifier (\S\ref{sec:phase-seg}), then apply a phase-specific sparsity configuration derived from the severity gradient.
51	Whether such a controller can recover most of the compression benefit while avoiding the severity amplification in low-sparsity phases is an open empirical question.
52	
53	A second direction concerns completing the mechanistic picture.
54	The discrimination collapse component of our hypothesis is robust across models, but the entropy redistribution component is model-dependent (\S\ref{sec:analysis}).
55	Directly measuring per-head entropy shifts across architecturally distinct models---and identifying what training-time properties (e.g., distillation depth, RLHF intensity) determine whether entropy concentrates or disperses under head pruning---would clarify the boundary conditions of the full entropy-discrimination collapse mechanism.
56	
57	Finally, scaling the empirical methodology to larger models and diverse reasoning tasks would establish the generality of the phase-strategy interaction documented in this work.
58	
59	\subsection{Limitations}
60	\label{sec:limitations}
61	
62	Our study is bounded by three principal constraints.
63	First, both models share the Qwen2ForCausalLM architecture; cross-architecture validation (e.g., LLaMA~3, Mistral) remains future work.
64	Second, evaluation is limited to MATH-500---different reasoning tasks may induce different phase structures and severity profiles.
65	Third, all experiments are conducted at the 7B scale; whether the phase-modulated severity patterns persist at larger scales is untested.
66	Extended limitations and anticipated reviewer concerns are discussed in Appendix~\ref{app:limitations}.

Second, the gradient is \emph{phase-specific}: compound interaction concentrates in low-sparsity phases while high-sparsity phases exhibit near-zero compound interaction ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\text{high}} < 0.06$ at $s \leq 0.30$; at $s = 0.35$, high-phase II rises to $0.105$ in a supplementary experiment outside the main four-level range, indicating the onset of compound interaction even in high-sparsity phases at extreme pruning rates). % exp_id: bf16_importance_s015..s030, bf16_ds_imp_s035; high-phase medians: 0.006, 0.015, 0.032, 0.053; s035 II_high=0.1051
This asymmetry means that importance-based eviction is not uniformly fragile---it is selectively fragile in a phase-dependent manner.
Third, and most strikingly, a \emph{crossover} emerges: at $s{=}0.25$, importance-based eviction \emph{outperforms} random eviction in high-sparsity phases (median severity $0.032$ vs.\ $0.818$) yet \emph{underperforms} in low-sparsity phases ($7.196$ vs.\ $1.363$---a ${>}5{\times}$ severity inflation relative to random). % exp_id: bf16_importance_s025, bf16_ds_rand_s025; source: experiment_summary_table.json; high: imp=0.032, rand=0.818; low: imp=7.196, rand=1.363
The same strategy reverses direction across phases---a phenomenon that cannot be derived from the observation that ``importance scores are noisier when attention is diffuse.''

% REBUTTAL: (1) Qualitative direction ≠ quantitative structure: 69-274× amplification is two orders of magnitude, not marginal. (2) Phase-specific concentration + crossover cannot be predicted from single-layer entropy reasoning. (3) Random eviction's flat profile (~1×) shows the amplification is strategy-specific, not an inherent property of compound sparsity.

\paragraph{Random masking as a falsification control.}
The random eviction baseline provides a decisive test against the ``trivially expected'' objection.
If compound severity amplification were an inherent property of applying two compression methods jointly---rather than an emergent phase-strategy interaction---random eviction should exhibit a comparable phase gradient.
It does not: random eviction fails seven of eight paired permutation tests across both models (7/8 FAIL); the single exception (Qwen $s{=}0.30$, $p{=}0.012$) exhibits negligible effect size ($d_z{=}{-}0.04$), producing no practically meaningful phase-modulated severity. % exp_id: bf16_ds_rand_s015..s030, bf16_qw_rand_s015..s030; verdict: 7/8 FAIL, 1 PASS (qw_rand_s030 p=0.012 d=-0.035 negligible)
The absence of a phase gradient under random masking isolates the amplification as strategy-specific: it arises from the interaction between importance-based eviction and phase structure, not from compound sparsity per se.

\paragraph{Cross-model replication and magnitude asymmetry.}
The phase-strategy interaction replicates across both models with perfect ordinal agreement: the Spearman rank correlation of paired $d_z$ effect sizes across sparsity levels is $\rho{=}1.0$, and a gradient permutation test confirms this monotonic co-escalation ($p{=}0.043$). % exp_id: cross_model_correlation; Spearman rho=1.0, gradient_perm p=0.043
All eight paired Wilcoxon tests (4 sparsity levels $\times$ 2 models) reject $H_0$, confirming the pattern is not an artifact of a single model's weight structure.

The \emph{magnitude} of the effect, however, differs substantially.
Qwen's median severity differences ($0.04 \to 0.23 \to 1.27 \to 2.94$) are approximately one-fifth of DeepSeek's ($0.39 \to 1.48 \to 7.16 \to 14.59$), and the onset threshold differs: DeepSeek's gradient is significant from $s{=}0.15$ (paired $d_z{=}0.44$), while Qwen's becomes clearly significant only at $s \geq 0.20$ ($d_z{=}0.55$; $s{=}0.15$ is borderline at $d_z{=}0.28$ with CI crossing zero). % exp_id: cohens_d_bf16.json (ds d_z: 0.4416,0.5195,0.6831,0.8031), cohens_d_bf16_qwen.json (qw d_z: 0.2811,0.5494,0.8894,1.0220).
The two models share the Qwen2ForCausalLM architecture but differ in training: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B is distilled from a larger reasoning model, while Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct undergoes standard instruction tuning.
We conjecture that distillation amplifies the phase-strategy interaction by producing sharper internal phase transitions---a hypothesis testable by comparing distilled and non-distilled variants at matched scale.

\paragraph{Mechanistic evidence: discrimination collapse as the robust signal.}
The entropy-discrimination collapse hypothesis (\S\ref{sec:analysis}) receives partial cross-model support.
The discrimination components---Gini coefficient reduction and coefficient-of-variation compression under compound sparsity---are directionally consistent across both models, confirming that importance-based eviction loses discriminative power in low-sparsity phases regardless of training procedure.
However, the entropy component is model-dependent: DeepSeek exhibits consistent negative entropy shifts (attention concentrates further under head pruning), while Qwen shows a sign reversal at $s{=}0.25$ ($\Delta H {=} {+}0.045$) and near-zero shift at $s{=}0.30$ ($\Delta H {=} {-}0.007$). % exp_id: mechanism_entropy_qwen; s025: +0.045, s030: -0.007
This divergence suggests that discrimination collapse---not entropy redistribution---is the primary driver of the phase-strategy interaction, with entropy behavior being a model-dependent secondary effect.
We therefore characterize the mechanistic evidence as \emph{preliminary}: the discrimination pathway is robust across models, but the complete entropy-discrimination collapse narrative requires the qualification that its entropy component does not generalize.

\paragraph{Implications for compound sparsity deployment.}
Our findings suggest that the standard practice of applying a uniform compression budget across all inference steps is suboptimal for reasoning models.
Compound severity is not distributed evenly: it concentrates in low-sparsity phases, where the entropy-discrimination collapse mechanism (\S\ref{sec:analysis}) renders importance-based eviction unreliable.
A deployment pipeline that allocates the same sparsity level $s$ to every token position implicitly accepts order-of-magnitude severity penalties during the exploratory reasoning stages that happen to fall in the low-sparsity regime.

This observation motivates \emph{phase-aware compression budgets}: rather than a single global sparsity target, the system would allocate higher capacity (lower sparsity) to low-sparsity phases---where compound interaction is most severe---and reclaim that budget in high-sparsity phases, where compound behavior is near-additive and importance-based eviction remains effective.
The severity gradient $G$ reported in \S\ref{sec:phase-amplification} provides a natural signal for such allocation: phases with $G \gg 1$ receive a reduced sparsity budget, while phases with $G \leq 1$ tolerate aggressive compression with minimal quality loss.

\paragraph{Future directions.}
The phase-aware allocation principle above points toward a concrete system design: a \emph{phase-gated controller} that monitors attention sparsity statistics in real time and dynamically adjusts the compound sparsity budget per reasoning phase.
The controller would route each generation step through a low-overhead phase classifier (\S\ref{sec:phase-seg}), then apply a phase-specific sparsity configuration derived from the severity gradient.
Whether such a controller can recover most of the compression benefit while avoiding the severity amplification in low-sparsity phases is an open empirical question.

A second direction concerns completing the mechanistic picture.
The discrimination collapse component of our hypothesis is robust across models, but the entropy redistribution component is model-dependent (\S\ref{sec:analysis}).
Directly measuring per-head entropy shifts across architecturally distinct models---and identifying what training-time properties (e.g., distillation depth, RLHF intensity) determine whether entropy concentrates or disperses under head pruning---would clarify the boundary conditions of the full entropy-discrimination collapse mechanism.

Finally, scaling the empirical methodology to larger models and diverse reasoning tasks would establish the generality of the phase-strategy interaction documented in this work.

\subsection{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

Our study is bounded by three principal constraints.
First, both models share the Qwen2ForCausalLM architecture; cross-architecture validation (e.g., LLaMA~3, Mistral) remains future work.
Second, evaluation is limited to MATH-500---different reasoning tasks may induce different phase structures and severity profiles.
Third, all experiments are conducted at the 7B scale; whether the phase-modulated severity patterns persist at larger scales is untested.
Extended limitations and anticipated reviewer concerns are discussed in Appendix~\ref{app:limitations}.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We presented an empirical investigation of how compound sparsity severity---the super-additive interaction between attention head pruning and KV cache eviction---varies across reasoning phases and eviction strategies in 7B-parameter language models. Our central finding is that compound severity is not a fixed property of the sparsity level but an emergent phase-strategy interaction whose magnitude spans over an order of magnitude within a single generation.

Our contributions, mapped to confirmed claims, are:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Strategy dependence (C1).} Compound severity depends qualitatively on the eviction strategy: importance-based eviction produces phase-modulated interaction (median phase difference $0.39$--$14.59$), while random eviction shows no significant phase modulation in 7/8 conditions (the sole exception---Qwen $s{=}0.30$, $p{=}0.012$, $d_z{=}{-}0.04$---has negligible effect size).

    \item \textbf{Phase modulation (C2).} Under importance-based eviction, the median Interaction Index difference between low- and high-sparsity phases increases monotonically with sparsity (Bonferroni-corrected $p < 0.005$ at all four levels), with paired effect sizes growing from $d_z{=}0.44$ (small) to $d_z{=}0.80$ (large).

    \item \textbf{Phase-strategy crossover (C3).} At $s{=}0.25$, importance-based eviction simultaneously outperforms random in high-sparsity phases ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}} = 0.032$ vs.\ $0.818$) and underperforms in low-sparsity phases ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}} = 7.196$ vs.\ $1.363$)---a qualitative reversal in strategy ranking.

    \item \textbf{Sub-exponential growth (C6).} The severity gradient grows with sparsity but at a decelerating rate, suggesting a natural ceiling on phase-dependent amplification.

    \item \textbf{Cross-model replication (C5).} The monotonic gradient replicates on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct at $s \geq 0.20$ ($d_z \geq 0.55$; Spearman $\rho = 1.0$ across sparsity levels; gradient permutation $p = 0.043$), with attenuated absolute magnitude (${\sim}1/5$ of DeepSeek).

    \item \textbf{Mechanistic explanation (C4).} Discrimination collapse---whereby head pruning degrades the discriminative power of importance scores---is robustly confirmed across both models (Gini and CV decrease in all 16 conditions). A secondary entropy redistribution pattern is consistent for DeepSeek but partially replicates on Qwen (2/4 conditions), indicating model-dependent modulation.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Limitations.}
Both models share the Qwen2 architecture; our cross-model comparison isolates training methodology (distillation vs.\ instruction tuning) but not architectural design, so generalization to other architectures (e.g., LLaMA, Mistral, multi-latent attention) remains open.
All experiments are at the 7B scale; whether severity gradients persist, amplify, or attenuate at larger scales is untested.
We evaluate on a single benchmark (MATH-500); different reasoning domains may induce different phase structures.
The discrimination collapse mechanism is supported by correlational evidence but lacks direct causal validation through controlled entropy manipulation.
While discrimination collapse (Gini and CV reduction) is consistent across all conditions for both models, the entropy redistribution component replicates on only 2 of 4 sparsity levels for Qwen, suggesting model-specific factors modulate its manifestation.

\paragraph{Future work.}
A \emph{phase-gated sparsity controller} that dynamically adjusts compound sparsity budgets per reasoning phase could mitigate the severity amplification we document while preserving compression gains where compound behavior is near-additive.
Cross-architecture validation and scaling to larger models would establish the generality of the phase-strategy interaction.
Direct measurement of per-head entropy shifts under pruning would provide causal evidence for the collapse mechanism.
